segments.title: Oil, territory, and global naval reach
segments.summary: The campaign map shows why access to oil and dispersed territories shape where fleets can operate and expand.
segments.body: The campaign map puts oil-producing regions and distant bases at the centre of fleet planning. Possession of places such as Persia and Pearl Harbor creates practical naval reach instead of merely raising a territorial score. Oil supports sustained operations, while dispersed ports give ships useful positions across several theatres. The scenario shows how fuel access, geography, and overseas possessions constrain a global fleet.

evidence.note: The campaign recap connects oil, controlled territory, Pearl Harbor, and future invasions.

segments.title: Fast battlecruisers as a hunting force
segments.summary: A group of 32-knot battlecruisers is organized to find and overwhelm a weaker enemy force while destroyers screen it.
segments.body: The campaign fleet is built around speed, with the battlecruisers detached to hunt while smaller ships take scouting and screening roles. Six 32-knot capital ships pursue the target, while Renown and its destroyers follow behind. This organization separates the striking force from the ships that find threats and guard heavier units. Speed can turn a nominal engagement into a pursuit the weaker side cannot escape.

evidence.note: He describes battlecruisers built to battlecruiser standards, their 32-knot speed, and assigns hunting, scouting, and screening roles.

segments.title: Speed and concentration against isolated cruisers
segments.summary: A concentrated battlecruiser-and-destroyer force illustrates how badly isolated cruisers fare when outnumbered and outrun.
segments.body: The game encounter emphasizes force concentration rather than a balanced duel. Six battlecruisers, another heavy ship, and a destroyer screen close on a single cruiser. Their speed margin prevents the target from choosing the terms of contact or escaping once found. It is a watch point on the tactical value of pairing fast heavy ships with smaller escorts and applying overwhelming local strength.

evidence.note: The opposing cruiser faces six battlecruisers, another battlecruiser, and destroyers; Dr. Clarke compares the odds to roughly twenty to one.

segments.title: Grouping fast battlecruisers against a battleship
segments.summary: Against a battleship, six battlecruisers are reorganized into two groups of three so speed and concentrated fire can be applied without one unwieldy formation.
segments.body: The appearance of an enemy battleship changes how the force is divided. Six battlecruisers form two groups of three instead of three pairs, and Renown receives a destroyer escort. The arrangement keeps several heavy ships together while preserving the ability to approach from more than one direction. Because the opposing battleship is limited to about 19.6 knots, the faster capital ships can choose the geometry of the engagement and concentrate their fire.

evidence.note: He responds to an enemy battleship by dividing six battlecruisers into two groups of three and assigning Renown a destroyer escort.
The opposing battleship's 19.6-knot speed leaves the faster battlecruisers able to dictate the engagement.

segments.title: Forming a battle line for accurate gunfire
segments.summary: The engagement demonstrates how a battle line, controlled speed, and a broadside create a decisive gunnery advantage.
segments.body: The battle line advances abreast and slows once close enough to improve accuracy. Its broadside combines thirteen-and-a-half-inch, six-inch, and four-inch guns. As the target runs parallel to one group, other ships close from another direction and create a drawn-out pincer. Formation, speed control, arcs of fire, and positional pressure produce an advantage that a ship-stat screen alone cannot explain.

evidence.note: He orders a line abreast, slows for accuracy, describes the broadside, and identifies the resulting pincer.

segments.title: Balancing naval budgets against growth and unrest
segments.summary: A campaign decision links naval spending to economic growth, political stability, and institutional prestige.
segments.body: A campaign event offers three competing outcomes: increase the naval budget, preserve naval prestige, or cut expenditure to promote GDP growth and reduce unrest. The economic and political benefit wins because the immediate naval cost is small. The decision makes fleet finance part of wider state capacity instead of an isolated shipbuilding total. Naval ambition has to compete with prosperity, domestic stability, and other claims on government resources.

evidence.note: He compares naval-budget, naval-prestige, GDP-growth, and unrest effects before choosing the economic option.

segments.title: Renown's reconnaissance design closes the escape route
segments.summary: An older battlecruiser and ten destroyers overtake a lone cruiser, showing what an 11-knot speed advantage means in practice.
segments.body: Renown leads its own group of ten destroyers against a single Austrian cruiser. As one of the original campaign battlecruisers, it carries six six-inch guns and was designed when reconnaissance was the main role. The cruiser can make only 21.5 knots while the attackers close at 32.5, leaving no realistic escape once contact is made. Its 8.4-inch guns are also unlikely to trouble armour rated up to 13.4 inches. The encounter keeps the game scenario separate from real history while showing how scouting speed, protection, and escort strength can turn detection into an inescapable pursuit.

evidence.note: A lone Austrian cruiser faces Renown and its ten destroyers, and Renown is identified as an original reconnaissance-role battlecruiser with six six-inch guns.
The cruiser makes 21.5 knots against a 32.5-knot pursuit, while its 8.4-inch guns face armour rated up to 13.4 inches.

segments.title: Building a home-defence fleet and submarine mass
segments.summary: Ships shift toward home defence while a large submarine force provides mass in reserve.
segments.body: After declining a risky battle, the campaign fleet redistributes battlecruisers for home defence. The choice distinguishes having enough strength available from accepting every engagement the game offers. Eighty newly available E-class submarines provide reserve mass, with further construction deferred until the next technological improvement. The fleet plan balances immediate readiness, risk, and modernization.

evidence.note: He assembles a home-defence fleet and reports eighty E-class submarines in service.

segments.title: Scrapping obsolete craft while retaining useful battlecruisers
segments.summary: A fleet review distinguishes obsolete small craft from older battlecruisers that remain capable enough to justify retention.
segments.body: The fleet review begins by age, and obsolete torpedo boats and other small craft are scrapped immediately. The same rule is not applied mechanically to the 1902 battlecruisers because several have been modernized and still fill useful roles. Chronological age does not equal practical obsolescence when a hull's capabilities and task still justify its cost. Selective retirement preserves useful strength while newer construction catches up with demand.

evidence.note: He scraps old torpedo boats and small craft but retains modernized battlecruisers from 1902 because they remain useful.

segments.title: Why refit older capital ships?
segments.summary: Older battlecruisers and battleships remain useful when refits preserve the tonnage needed for battles and invasions.
segments.body: Older capital ships can remain useful after a limited refit. An upgraded 13.5-inch battery keeps the ship relevant, while the hull supplies the raw tonnage that campaign invasions and battles require. These vessels do not need to be first-line units, only capable enough to contribute without making a loss strategically painful. The refit limits speed, armour, and expense instead of trying to turn an old battleship into a new design.

evidence.note: He explains that upgraded older ships provide required operational tonnage, then limits the refit's speed, armour, and cost while making the battleships useful again.

segments.title: Combining armour, speed, and heavy guns
segments.summary: Two campaign designs explore the trade-offs and attractions of high speed, heavy armour, and exceptionally large broadsides.
segments.body: The King Edward VII design combines 16.5-inch guns, a 17.3-inch belt, and 30 knots. It is meant to shock any opponent that encounters it. A second design pursues a fifteen-gun main broadside, heavy secondary fire, and twelve-inch belt protection across the ship. The game turns the trade-offs among firepower, protection, and speed into concrete design choices, with both extreme specifications kept firmly inside the campaign scenario.

evidence.note: He details the guns, belt armour, speed, and intended shock effect of two new capital-ship designs.

segments.title: Choosing battlecruisers for a global war
segments.summary: Battlecruiser construction suits a war fought across distant theatres rather than principally in the North Sea.
segments.body: The campaign's strategic logic rests on where the fighting occurs. Because most combat takes place around the wider world rather than in the North Sea, battlecruisers become the principal mobile heavy force. Their speed and capital-ship firepower suit hunting, reinforcement, and concentration across dispersed theatres in the game's alternate history. A warship type's value depends on the geography and missions a navy expects, as well as its place in a battle line.

evidence.note: He says the campaign war is being fought outside the North Sea and identifies battlecruisers as his resulting construction choice.

segments.title: Torpedo threats and destroyer screening
segments.summary: A close action shows destroyers making torpedo runs while a fast battlecruiser exploits damaged arcs and judges an enemy launch by its actual geometry.
segments.body: The enemy torpedo launch is a threat to evaluate rather than an automatic reason to break off. Furious approaches the opponent's more damaged side, denying a symmetrical exchange and keeping the better firing position. The destroyer screen also makes torpedo runs, but poor British torpedo technology limits what those attacks can achieve. Furious then steers inside an ineffective enemy track. The opposing cruiser is substantial but looks small beside Furious, itself not among the campaign's largest battlecruisers, which gives the action a useful sense of scale.

evidence.note: The battle covers enemy and destroyer torpedo runs, an approach on the opponent's more damaged side, inadequate British torpedo technology, and a turn inside an ineffective torpedo track.

segments.title: Searching through fog with battlecruisers
segments.summary: Six fast battlecruisers adapt their formation and speed while searching for an enemy concealed by fog.
segments.body: In poor visibility, six fast battlecruisers try to form a line-abreast search formation. Their speed drops so lagging ships can catch up before the group moves forward again. The result is an improvised staggered V rather than the intended textbook line, while the enemy uses the fog bank to avoid detection. Visibility, formation keeping, scouting width, and speed control become parts of the same tactical problem.

evidence.note: He sets six 32-knot battlecruisers line abreast in fog, slows them to reform, and searches for the hidden enemy.

segments.title: Comparing national strength before a naval war
segments.summary: A British-German comparison shows why budgets, industry, fleet composition, tonnage, and readiness all matter before judging naval odds.
segments.body: The campaign comparison with Germany goes well beyond battleship count. Britain's GDP is roughly three times larger, its oil production about five times larger, and its naval budget nearly eight times larger. Britain has 30 battleships to Germany's 15 and 60 battlecruisers to Germany's one, while Germany has more cruisers. The game also tracks population, army budgets, available funds, crew pools, construction, repairs, and total tonnage. These alternate-history figures show how resources, readiness, and force mix shape strategic confidence.

evidence.note: He compares British and German population, GDP, oil, budgets, fleet counts, construction, readiness, and tonnage before judging the likely war.

segments.title: Why all-big-gun ships still need smaller guns
segments.summary: Rapid-fire secondary guns remain necessary to counter destroyers and torpedo boats.
segments.body: The game prompt leads to a useful corrective about the all-big-gun battleship. HMS Dreadnought retained smaller weapons because destroyers and torpedo boats demanded a faster-firing answer. The phrase "all-big-gun" is advertising shorthand rather than a literal description of every weapon aboard. A capital ship's main battery did not replace the need for close-range defence against small, fast attackers.

evidence.note: He cites Dreadnought's smaller guns as protection against destroyers and torpedo boats.

segments.title: Choosing Indian Ocean objectives against Japan
segments.summary: Arabia and Madagascar are prioritized as objectives because taking them would remove Japanese-held positions from the Indian Ocean.
segments.body: Japanese-held territories are judged by how much they would change the campaign's strategic geography. Arabia and Madagascar take priority because capturing them would remove Japanese positions from the Indian Ocean. Attacking those colonies is explicitly separated from invading Japan itself. Although these holdings belong to the game's alternate history, the reasoning mirrors a real planning problem: an objective matters for the access and regional control it provides, as well as the territory gained.

evidence.note: He identifies Arabia and Madagascar as objectives for clearing Japanese-held positions from the Indian Ocean and distinguishes those colonies from Japan itself.

segments.title: Concentrating forces before a northern Japan campaign
segments.summary: Battleships, battlecruisers, and destroyers are drawn from dispersed stations before an attack on northern Japan becomes practical.
segments.body: Battleships, battlecruisers, and destroyers move from several regions toward the prospective Japanese campaign. Some stations contain fewer ships than expected, so the plan has to be rebuilt from the forces actually available. Other powers move thousands of tons while Britain shifts millions, aiming to put enough shipping in the area to make an attack on northern Japan feasible. A distant objective becomes credible only after dispersed forces form a sustainable local concentration.

evidence.note: He transfers multiple ship types from scattered stations, describes moving millions of tons, and plans enough local strength to attack northern Japan.

segments.title: When fleet demand outruns shipyard capacity
segments.summary: An overloaded construction program forces attention to industrial capacity and research priorities, including anti-submarine warfare.
segments.body: Campaign shipbuilding capacity is completely overwhelmed even as naval funds grow. More money and fresh designs cannot produce usable ships faster than the available yards can build them. Research spending also follows operational need: an anti-submarine warfare improvement is chosen after a weakness there becomes apparent. The watch point connects procurement ambition to dockyard bottlenecks and an identified shortfall.

evidence.note: He links fleet demand to overloaded shipbuilding capacity, invests in supporting technology, and selects ASW research to address a weakness.

segments.title: Using an alliance to cover another theatre
segments.summary: The French alliance lets Britain concentrate against Japan while treating Germany as a lower immediate priority.
segments.body: After concentrating against Japan, Britain can accept more risk elsewhere in the campaign. The alliance with France makes Germany a lower immediate priority because French military strength is being maintained. Allied capacity substitutes for forces Britain would otherwise need to hold back. The scenario shows how alliances redistribute risk and permit concentration in a chosen theatre.

evidence.note: He says the French alliance lets him ignore Germany for the moment because France is investing in its military.

segments.title: Reinforcing a distant fleet after attrition
segments.summary: Repairs and losses force destroyers and battlecruisers to be pulled from Malacca, Cuba, and other stations to sustain the Japanese campaign.
segments.body: After the first engagements, 82 percent of the forward force is refitting or repairing, so replacements have to come from the wider map. Destroyers leave Malacca, while battlecruisers move from other stations, including Cuba. Winning battles does not end the operational problem because damaged units create an immediate demand for fresh hulls and escorts. In the campaign's alternate geography, reinforcing one theatre also thins forces elsewhere, making global fleet distribution part of the cost of sustained operations.

evidence.note: With much of the forward fleet refitting or repairing, he sends destroyers from Malacca and moves battlecruisers from Cuba and other stations to reinforce the theatre.
